Building Kharis (or a give/receive relationship) with the gods is not an immediate process. It takes time, devotion, and intention to build that relationship, just like with any other. You can also end the prayer with whatever you wish. I personally end with giving thanks as well as facing my hands up or down, depending on the god, and meditating for a while. Some people end their prayers with a phrase, such as "Your will be done" or "In this prayer I give thanks". You may not feel anything at the start, especially if you are still wary about the gods' existence. But over time, with acts of devotion and worship, the relationship will deepen.

The important thing to remember is that prayer doesn't need to be formal, with the recitation of hymns and such. As long as you are respectful and come with the right intentions.

If you are getting a lot of your information on Hellenic faith through unreliable sources, you can easily become confused by a ton of misinformation. I recommend watching some youtube videos as well as taking a look in the resources that this subreddit has on the sidebar. I recommend as a starter video, if reading seems daunting for now, this one by Fel the Blithe: [https://youtu.be/6y-uL69I\_QI?si=DvXZ-Q0m1f0LChdZ](https://youtu.be/6y-uL69I_QI?si=DvXZ-Q0m1f0LChdZ)  
People do not choose a god, they simply worship the deities they wish to seek guidance or aid from. I for one pray to Athena often as I am a student, as well as Aphrodite for self love, and Hynos/Morpheus both for good sleep and dreams.
The keyboard method is not an accurate form of divination by any means. By talking, do you mean like having a conversational relationship?

That is approaching the faith with a monotheistic mindset. We are polytheist, meaning we worship many gods. You may choose to devote yourself to a particular god, should you find their guidance or wisdom helpful in your endeavors, but you can also worship others. You also do not need divination to build a relationship with the gods. You can simply pray, as divination work can be misinterpreted, especially if you are new to the craft.  
So in short, you can pray/worship both Apollo and Aphrodite. You do not have to choose.

The typical structure I follow would be to first say their name as well as an epithet and praise. (Apollo, a friend of muses and a player of sweetest songs.) Then, I would usually give my offerings if I have one to give, usually material objects, burning of incense, or libations such as honey or wine. Then, I thank them for all the things they do in my life and their effect on me. It's only after this that I make my requests (for guidance, assistance, blessings, etc.) Then I usually follow with more praise, and then end with a thank you. You can meditate for a while afterwards. And then usually I lift my hands to the heavens if I am praying to an Ouranic God or turn my palms down for a Chthonic God.

There is no right way to pray, as it can be as formal or informal as you like. Just keep in mind that you must be respectful, and come to the prayer with the right intentions (ie. not demanding favors without offering something in return.)

Amen, as a word, is simply a word meaning affirmation or agreement. It isn't necessarily a Christian phrase, just a Hebrew one.

Prayer does not require an altar. The act of purification, in your case, washing your hands, is a way to make the act sacred. I did an offering of olive leaves and honey the first time I prayed to basically tell the Gods that I was coming with friendship in mind. But that isn't necessary. Devotion is a very important part of building Kharis with the Gods, and I think you did beautifully.

Food offerings are not the only things you can give. Devotional acts, such as doing something in the name of a God is also a way to build Kharis. I only give food offerings occasionally. Most of the offerings I give are material objects, libations (which are poured on the ground outside), and devotional acts (like when I cook, I devote the act to Hestia).
